abstract.p: This epitaph commemorates Lady Waller by addressing the reader directly and asserting the enduring nature of her virtue. It presents her as perpetually worthy of mourning and describes her life as marked by devotion to God. She is explicitly likened to a saint, and the poem concludes with wordplay on her name, associating it with a laurel tree to suggest honour and lasting renown.

lg.l: All worthy eies reade this that hither come;
Never decaying vertue fills this Toombe:
Never enough to bee lamented heere,
As long as women kind are worth a teare.
Within these weeping stones lies Lady Waller,
Her life was so good whylst while shee liv’d here,
Leaveled so straight to God in love and feare:
Even so good that turne her name, and see
Ready to Crowne that life a Lawrell=Tree.

div.head: Historical context and dating
div.p: Anne (Anna) Choute Waller (d. September 1624) was the wife of Sir Walter Waller (d. 1599). She was buried in the chancel of St Mary the Virgin, Speldhurst, Kent, where an elaborate alabaster monument was erected to commemorate her. The text of this poem is also found on the monument (see ).

div.head: Notes
div.p: In both copies, the poem is transmitted alongside a companion poem on Sir Walter Waller, together forming a paired set of elegies on husband and wife ().
